provisionalMaterialIssues: The claim that spare breaker spaces do not establish service capacity, and the proposed nameplate/service-load assessment as the way to determine capacity, are not supported by the supplied text. PC § 502.1 (sourceID research-permitext_discovered-id:12072-4) refers electrical requirements to the NYC Electrical Code but provides no service-capacity test or calculation. These claims are practical guidance, not claims of mandatory law, but remain unsupported by the supplied evidence.

The recommendation to use 208 V is unsupported by the supplied sources. BC 2702.1.7 (sourceID research-permitext_discovered-id:5370-3) concerns emergency and standby power feeders, not voltage-drop calculations; BC 2702.1.7.1 (sourceID research-permitext_cross_reference-id:5371-1) concerns feeder location.

The advice to use 120 V and account for neutral and load distribution for particular loads is also not established by any supplied source. No cited source addresses voltage-drop formulas or their application to a four-wire 120/208 V feeder.

rejectedDraftAssessment.reason: The answer gives a useful, appropriately qualified ventilation approach: MC 401.2 supports natural-plus-exhaust or mechanical ventilation pathways, and the cited outdoor-air provisions support designing for required outdoor air. But it also applies Fuel Gas Code makeup-air provisions to the home's existing exhaust fans without establishing that those fans fall within the Fuel Gas Code's scope. The supplied scope provision, FGC 301.1, limits that chapter to equipment and appliances that are part of installations regulated by that code; FGC 304.4.1 specifically addresses exhaust fans in the context of fuel-burning devices. That leaves the answer's project-specific claim about replacement air for all existing fans unsupported as stated.
materialIssues: The statement that the existing kitchen and bath exhaust fans require replacement air under FGC 304.9.1 is presented as applicable to this house without establishing the provision's applicability to those fans. FGC 301.1 (sourceID research-permitext_cross_reference-id:8022-chapter-scope-01) supplies a scope limitation, while FGC 304.4.1 (sourceID research-permitext_discovered-id:8085-4) expressly addresses makeup air and calculations for fuel-burning devices. The answer should limit this conclusion to fans covered by the Fuel Gas Code or identify the applicability question.
missingSources: Project-specific information establishing whether FGC 304.9.1 applies to the existing kitchen and bath exhaust fans, including their relationship to the fuel-burning-device installation.
MC Section 402, for the detailed natural-ventilation opening requirements, and MC Section 403.1, referenced by the R-2 table footnote for the airflow relationship.

provisionalMaterialIssues: The Type II requirement is stated without its express no-grease-or-smoke condition. Source ID research-permitext_discovered-id:10677-9 (MC § 507.3) limits that requirement to appliances producing heat or moisture without producing grease or smoke. The answer says the emissions are not established, so it cannot conclude that the Type II rule applies to this installation on the stated facts.

The answer understates the alternative Type I trigger by saying Type I rules “may” apply if the appliance produces grease or smoke. Source ID research-permitext_discovered-id:10665-1 (MC § 507.2) says Type I hoods shall be installed where cooking appliances produce grease or smoke. This matters because the answer presents Type II as the general requirement without clearly making it conditional on the absence of those emissions.

rejectedDraftAssessment.reason: The answer gives a supported, conditional response rather than a categorical yes or no. BC §§ 1006.3 and 1006.3.1 establish an occupied-roof egress framework, and § 1006.3.2 allows a single exit only when a listed condition applies. The answer correctly identifies the missing occupant-load, story, stair-access, and exception facts and does not claim that a second exit must specifically be a stair. Its qualifications matter for this converted-loft project.
